title: Index Maintenance vs Actual Query Performance
description: Learn why index fragmentation does not always hurt performance, how to measure real query impact, and how to build a rational index maintenance strategy.

data.text: For years, the standard advice for SQL Server index maintenance was simple: rebuild indexes when fragmentation exceeds 30%, reorganize when it exceeds 5% and is below 30%, and run this on a weekly or nightly schedule. But modern SQL Server versions, faster storage, and larger datasets have changed the calculus. **Index fragmentation is often not the performance problem you think it is.**

This lesson examines the relationship between index maintenance and actual query performance, teaches you how to measure fragmentation's real impact, and helps you design a maintenance strategy that improves performance without wasting I/O and CPU on unnecessary rebuilds.

Fragmentation occurs when the logical order of index pages does not match the physical order on disk. There are two types: **internal fragmentation** (pages with empty space) and **external fragmentation** (pages out of order on disk). Internal fragmentation wastes space and increases I/O. External fragmentation causes extra disk head movement on spinning drives.

terms.definition: Wasted space within index pages caused by page splits during inserts and updates. Measured as avg_page_space_used_in_percent in sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats.
Pages that are out of physical order on disk, causing extra I/O to read them sequentially. Measured as avg_fragmentation_in_percent.
When SQL Server inserts a row into a full index page, it splits the page into two and moves half the rows to a new page. Page splits cause fragmentation and are expensive.
The percentage of space to fill each index page during creation or rebuild. Lower fill factors reduce page splits but increase storage and I/O.

data.text: The answer depends on your storage. On spinning disks (HDDs), external fragmentation causes physical head movement and can significantly slow range scans. On SSDs and NVMe, random I/O is much faster, so external fragmentation has minimal impact. Internal fragmentation is always bad: it increases the number of pages SQL Server must read, which increases logical reads and CPU usage.

cards.title: HDD Storage
cards.description: Sequential I/O is much faster than random I/O. External fragmentation causes head movement, making range scans slower. Rebuilds at moderate fragmentation levels can improve performance.
pros: Fragmentation impact is measurable and significant
cons: Rebuilds are expensive in terms of I/O and CPU
Frequent rebuilds may not be worth the gain

cards.title: SSD / NVMe Storage
cards.description: Random I/O is fast and sequential I/O advantage is small. External fragmentation has minimal performance impact. Internal fragmentation still wastes space and increases logical reads.
pros: Fragmentation matters less for scan performance
Fewer rebuilds needed; lower maintenance overhead
cons: Internal fragmentation still increases I/O volume
Page splits still cause write amplification

data.text: Instead of maintaining indexes based solely on fragmentation thresholds, measure the actual impact on your queries. Use Query Store or DMVs to identify indexes with high modification counts and query those specific indexes to see if fragmentation correlates with slow performance.

data.title: Identify Indexes That Actually Need Maintenance
data.content: Use sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats and physical stats to find indexes with high writes and high fragmentation together — not just fragmentation alone.
data.code:
SELECT 
    OBJECT_NAME(i.object_id) AS table_name,
    i.name AS index_name,
    i.type_desc,
    ps.avg_fragmentation_in_percent,
    ps.page_count,
    us.user_seeks,
    us.user_scans,
    us.user_lookups,
    us.user_updates,
    CAST(ps.page_count * 8.0 / 1024 AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS size_mb
FROM sys.indexes AS i
INNER JOIN sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats(DB_ID(), NULL, NULL, NULL, 'LIMITED') AS ps
    ON i.object_id = ps.object_id AND i.index_id = ps.index_id
INNER JOIN sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats AS us
    ON i.object_id = us.object_id AND i.index_id = us.index_id
WHERE ps.page_count > 1000
  AND us.user_updates > 1000
  AND ps.avg_fragmentation_in_percent > 10
ORDER BY us.user_updates DESC;

data.title: Rebuild Only What Matters
data.text: An index with 80% fragmentation but zero reads and 10 million writes per day is a maintenance nightmare, not a performance problem. Prioritize indexes that are both fragmented and actively used by queries.

Index rebuild drops and recreates the index, fully compacting pages and removing fragmentation. It is an offline operation by default (though ONLINE = ON is available in Enterprise Edition). Index reorganize defragments the leaf level of the index in-place without dropping it. Reorganize is always online but is less thorough.

rows: High — full table copy in tempdb

data.text: A rational index maintenance strategy balances the cost of rebuilds against the performance benefit. The goal is not perfectly defragmented indexes — it is fast queries. Measure query performance before and after maintenance, adjust thresholds based on your storage and workload, and consider skipping maintenance entirely for tables that change rarely.

data.title: Maintenance Strategy Guidelines
items: Measure query performance with Query Store or Extended Events — if queries are fast, do not rebuild
Rebuild only indexes with page_count > 1000 and avg_fragmentation_in_percent > 30% (or your measured threshold)
Reorganize indexes with fragmentation between 5% and 30% only if they are actively scanned
Skip maintenance for read-only or rarely-modified indexes — fragmentation cannot hurt what is never read
Use ONLINE = REBUILD for Enterprise Edition during business hours; schedule offline rebuilds for maintenance windows
Monitor tempdb usage during rebuilds — large offline rebuilds consume tempdb space

data.title: Maintenance Windows Are Not Free
data.text: Index rebuilds are I/O and CPU intensive. Running them during peak hours can degrade query performance for active users. Always schedule heavy maintenance during defined maintenance windows and monitor tempdb growth.

items.question: Should I rebuild all indexes every night?
items.answer: No. Rebuilding all indexes every night is a legacy practice from the SQL Server 2005 era. Modern best practice is to measure fragmentation and usage, then rebuild only the indexes that benefit. Many production databases run with zero index rebuilds and still perform well.

items.question: What fill factor should I use?
items.answer: The default fill factor of 0 (100%) is correct for most read-heavy tables. Use a lower fill factor (e.g., 80 or 90) only for tables with heavy page-split activity (many inserts into the middle of an index). Monitor page splits with sys.dm_db_index_operational_stats to decide.

items.question: Does rebuilding an index update statistics?
items.answer: Yes. Index rebuilds automatically update statistics with a full scan by default. Reorganize does not update statistics. If you rely on rebuilds for statistics maintenance, ensure your rebuild frequency is sufficient for your workload.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Fragmentation is not always the performance villain — on SSDs, external fragmentation has minimal impact
Internal fragmentation always hurts: it increases logical reads and wastes space regardless of storage type
Measure query performance, not just fragmentation percentages — rebuild indexes that are both fragmented and actively used
Rebuild is thorough but expensive and offline by default; reorganize is lightweight and always online
A rational strategy rebuilds only what needs rebuilding, at a frequency your storage and workload can tolerate
data.takeaway: Index maintenance should serve query performance, not the other way around. If your queries are fast, your maintenance is good enough.
